items.body: An advisory group is recommending Idaho use its opioid settlement funds to focus on at-risk populations and communities. (Getty Images) An advisory group has identified Idaho counties at high risk for opioid use disorder to target in its recommendations for the state’s use of opioid settlement funds. The Idaho Behavioral Health Council brings together the state’s three branches of government — legislative, judicial and executive — to provide recommendations to lawmakers about how to improve mental health and substance use issues statewide. The council on Friday finalized its recommendation that opioid settlement funds be prioritized for at-risk populations and communities. A summary highlighting some of the counties facing the highest risk of opioid use disorder included Kootenai, Benewah, Nez Perce, Bannock, Bear Lake, Clearwater, Boise and Ada counties. The state’s opioid settlement fund was created from a nationwide settlement with opioid manufacturers and may be used for certain, approved prevention or treatment projects. Last year, the Legislature approved spending $6.8 million of opioid settlement funds, according to a memo from the Division of Financial Management. Idaho Behavioral Health Council asks lawmakers to prioritize rural communities with opioid funding The council voted on its top priorities at a meeting in June, which included funding proposed for projects that focus on prevention for high-risk populations, behavioral health support for first responders, and developing the behavioral health workforce. Council members on Friday agreed to send a one-page summary outlining risk factors for opioid use disorder and highlighting which counties were most at-risk, using a 2024 report titled the Opioid-Related Overdose Vulnerability in Idaho: An Epidemiological Assessment. “This handout identifies risk factors for opioid use disorder and puts them in the context of Idaho, where those places are, where we may have more vulnerable folks, where we have had higher levels of overdose, where we have high levels of opioid prescriptions being written,” said Sara Omundson, administrative director of state courts and co-chair of the Behavioral Health Council. “All of this is based on research that was done over the last few years.” The council also agreed to ask the governor and state legislative budget writers to prioritize projects that serve rural communities in the state. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE What areas are at high risk for opioid use? Factors that may lead to certain populations to be at higher risk of misusing opioids include lower educational attainment, according to the risk factor summary the council included with its recommendations. Those without college experience are almost twice as likely to misuse opioids, the summary said. The summary also identified other Idaho counties at-risk because of factors such as high prescription rates and high narcotic arrests using data from the American Community Survey , the Idaho Prescription Drug Monitoring Program , and the Idaho State Police Statistical Analysis Center. The top counties at risk based on low average educational attainment are Shoshone, Lincoln, Minidoka, Owyhee, Adams, Benewah, Payette, Gooding, Jerome and Clark counties. The top counties for high opioid prescription rates are Nez Perce, Bannock, Bear Lake, Butte, Lewis, Shoshone, Benewah, Caribou, Gem and Lemhi. Brooke Green represents Idaho’s Legislative District 18 in the House. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Legislature) In general, people ages 26-49 are at the greatest risk of opioid misuse and overdose, the summary said. items.body: U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins (left) swears in Michael Boren as the under secretary for Natural Resources and Environment in her office on Jan. 20, 2026, at the USDA Headquarters in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Christophe Paul/U.S. Department of Agriculture) Three Democratic U.S. senators are demanding the Trump Administration investigate reports that Undersecretary of Agriculture for Natural Resources and Environment Michael Boren allegedly pushed officials for additional resources to fight a small wildfire near his Idaho ranch this summer. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE U.S. Sens. Ron Wyden, D-Oregon; Amy Klobuchar, D-Minnesota; and Martin Heinrich, D-New Mexico, requested a full investigation into Boren’s involvement and influence in the Cabin Creek Fire in a letter they sent to U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins. “Mr. Boren’s actions constitute potentially a misuse of taxpayer funds and put American families at further risk by diverting scarce resources from high-priority wildfires threatening communities elsewhere in the region and country,” the senators wrote. “We request a full investigation into the nature and extent of Boren’s involvement in response to the Cabin Creek Fire and a detailed accounting of the safeguards the agency has implemented or plans to implement to prevent political interference and conflicts of interest in wildfire response.” Need to get in touch? Have a news tip? CONTACT US Earlier this month, the Washington Post reported that Boren pushed U.S. Forest Service officials to increase the number of aircraft responding to a small fire near a ranch Boren owns in the Sawtooth National Recreation Area. “Western states are already facing a shortage of firefighting personnel and resources as a direct result of the Trump administration’s staffing and funding cuts,” the Democrats wrote in a press release issued Friday. “During this record setting fire season, fires of much larger size threatening American lives and homes have not received even a fraction of the same commitment of resources.” Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit legal watchdog group, has also called for an investigation into the allegations and filed a complaint with the Agriculture Department’s Office of Inspector General, according to an Aug. 17 press release. “The Inspector General must investigate whether Undersecretary Boren risked public safety to protect his property,” said CREW President Donald K. Sherman in the release. “Not only are Boren’s priorities in doubt, but his actions raise questions about his ‘scant’ qualifications for his role. His reported actions could be the result of incompetence, deliberate malfeasance or both. Regardless, they are inexcusable.” Boren is a founder of Clearwater Analytics, a Boise-based financial technology company. In 2025 President Donald Trump appointed Boren as undersecretary of natural resources and the environment at the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Mike Simpson, on Investigating the Crisis of Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women listen as Maulian Bryant (left) spoke about the challenges her Penobscot Nation faces in accessing resources to find missing people. From left to right: Mary Jane Miles, Cheryl Horn, Abigail Echo-Hawk and Eugenia Charles-Newton. (Screenshot via YouTube/House Appropriations Committee) Idaho Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson this year is looking to boost federal funding for tribes to address the ongoing Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons crisis. Chairman of the Interior, Environment and Related Agencies subcommittee U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson, R-Idaho, looks on during a House Appropriations Committee hearing at the Rayburn House Office Building on April 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Heather Diehl/Getty Images) Simpson chairs the Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies Subcommittee of the House Appropriations Committee. The subcommittee in June advanced a budget with a 26% increase to the Bureau of Indian Affairs, which includes: an additional $142 million for criminal investigations and police services $17 million for law enforcement special initiatives $33 million specifically for missing and murdered Indigenous women, which is about a $14.5 million increase over the fiscal year 2026 appropriation. $5 million for the use of forensic genealogy to identify missing and murdered individuals in unsolved cases through the bureau’s Operation Spirit Return. “We put a bunch more money into tribal justice, and that’s hard in a year when we’re trying to reduce spending at the federal level,” Simpson said in an interview. As a result, he said other portions of the budget, such as funding for the Bureau of Land Management, the U.S. Forest Service and the Smithsonian Institution all saw reductions. “But I’ve said from the beginning: We’re not going to try to balance the budget on the back of the tribes,” Simpson said. “These are trust and treaty responsibilities we’ve got with our Native American brothers and sisters, and we’ve got to keep those. ” Coeur d’Alene Tribe Chairman Chief J. Allan told the Idaho Capital Sun in an emailed statement that the tribe supports the effort. “The issue has gotten more attention in recent years, and Congressman Simpson recognizes that serious problems require adequate funding,” Allan said. “While the focus on MMIP is critical, he also recognizes that the tragic situation is the direct result of decades of public safety and justice deficiencies across Indian Country. Addressing those shortfalls across the system will help improve conditions overall, as well as prevent missing and murdered incidents in the future.” Marco Ovando, spokesman for the Shoshone-Paiute Tribes, said there was still a lot of work to be done to address the MMIP crisis. “The crisis of Missing and Murdered Indigenous People within Idaho and the United States is still largely being unaddressed despite national attention in recent years,” Ovando wrote in an emailed statement from the Tribes. “While the Idaho Legislature has created a taskforce in 2020 and a report 2021, state-tribal collaboration remains very limited. … We have a case as recent as this spring where the investigation has produced very little resulting in families without closure, frustrated leadership, and a community left on edge. We hope Congress will appropriate more funding to address these shortfalls because our people are tired of the pain and sorrow and lack of help.” Leaders from the Nez Perce, Shoshone-Bannock, and Kootenai Tribes could not be reached for comment. Members of the veterans group spent the year learning about crops, planting vegetables and caring for the garden, Case Manager Steve Mitchley said. In the first year of the garden’s existence, the veterans group harvested potatoes, onions, bell peppers, squash and beets. American Legion Post 113, A New Path Idaho and Lowe’s provided about $800 worth of donated materials to support the garden, officials said. Correction officials said that while the garden is small, it has grown into something much bigger by providing a sense of community service and hope. “This first season has been a valuable learning experience,” Mitchley said in a written statement. “The group hopes to expand the number of garden boxes next year.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. items.body: Melanie Folwell, lead organizer for the ballot initiative in Idaho to restore abortion access, speaks to supporters at the Idaho Capitol in July. The nonprofit she leads, Idahoans United for Women and Families, is suing the state over a final segment of ballot language that will also appear in the statewide voter pamphlet. (Photo by Kelcie Moseley-Morris/Stateline) BOISE, Idaho — The group leading the effort to restore abortion access by ballot initiative in Idaho has filed a lawsuit against state officials over proposed language that will appear on the ballot and in a state-issued voter pamphlet. Idahoans United for Women and Families, the nonprofit organization that drafted the initiative — now called Proposition 1 — says the “yes” and “no” statements as prepared by Idaho officials violate the law guiding the initiative process and are confusing and misleading. Attorneys filed the lawsuit to the Idaho Supreme Court late Wednesday night. Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane stressed that the issue needs to be quickly resolved to meet upcoming ballot deadlines. The voter pamphlet must be printed by September 25, according to the law, and ballots need to be mailed to military and overseas voters about a week before that. McGrane said the state has paused production amid the litigation on the 850,000 copies of the voter pamphlet that need to be printed and mailed. “There was a good-faith effort to try and reflect each of the sides of the pro and con statements that were submitted to us,” McGrane told Stateline by phone on Thursday. “I think one of the biggest challenges that we’re going to see with Proposition 1 is that it’s a very complicated issue with a lot of nuance … and this isn’t a simple issue to consolidate down into a short, one-sentence statement.” Following the law, McGrane developed the language for the statements with Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador, who has been outspoken in his anti-abortion views for many years and recently appealed a federal judge’s decision that would protect abortion access in cases of threats to a pregnant patient’s physical and mental health. Labrador told Stateline in an emailed statement that his duty alongside the secretary was to clearly and concisely explain the effects of a “yes” or “no” vote and to fully inform Idaho voters, and said they applied the same legal standard to every measure that has been on the ballot. “Idaho voters deserve a straightforward explanation of what their vote will do,” Labrador said. Idaho Supreme Court orders officials to revise abortion ballot initiative language, impact statement There have been similar legal fights over abortion ballot language in other states. Activists on both sides of the issue in Missouri, for example, have spent years arguing over ballot language , both on the 2024 citizen-led amendment that restored legal access to abortion, and on the 2026 amendment referred by the legislature that would reinstate the ban. Similar battles between Republican state officials and initiative organizers played out in Ohio , Arizona and Montana between 2023 and 2024. Voters in all three of those states ultimately approved amendments to protect abortion rights. It’s also not the first time Idahoans United for Women and Families has sued the state over ballot language. In April 2025, the Idaho Supreme Court heard arguments in the lawsuit, including whether the short ballot title and fiscal impact statement should be revised, and unanimously sided with Idahoans United on those two elements. Under Idaho law , the ballot must include a clear and concise statement about the effect of a “yes” or “no” vote, and the voter pamphlet must include a complete copy of the initiative text, its fiscal impact, and arguments for or against the measure with rebuttals. (Kevin Richert/Idaho EdNews) Heading to a meeting, flanked by House GOP Caucus Chair Jaron Crane, Moyle wasted no time getting to the point — Pemberton’s bill to rebrand Lewis-Clark State College as the state’s fourth full-fledged university. “He commented in passing that he hadn’t had time to ‘kill it yet,’” Pemberton, LC State’s president, said in subsequent emails to two other lawmakers. Pemberton stands by her account. When EdNews asked Moyle about the exchange this week, he chuckled. “She was persistent in the hallway all the time. I was just giving her a hard time.” Either way, the bill died, without a House hearing. Moyle, R-Star, insists he didn’t kill it, but says he doesn’t support the name change. Pemberton pledges to try again in 2027. “I better try one more time,” Pemberton said in an EdNews interview last week. “The campus community wants me to try again.” While renaming sounds cosmetic and simple, branding is essential. Supporters say university status better reflects a 133-year-old institution offering everything from associate’s degrees to master’s programs. A name is how an institution of higher learning markets itself to would-be students, prospective faculty members and possible business partners. A one-word change can change a lot. And the LC State renaming proposal was the most significant higher ed policy bill from the 2026 session. Emails between Pemberton and legislators — obtained by Idaho Education News through a public records request — offer an unusual and unfiltered behind-the-scenes look at how this bill died. The name change sailed through the Senate, but ran into high-placed resistance in the House, from Moyle and from his newly appointed House Education Committee chairman. LC State officials lobbied furiously to save their bill — working their skeptics, directly and indirectly — but to no avail. The case for the change With a freshly made video and handouts, and a webpage dedicated to the name change initiative , LC State is giving an updated look to the rebranding proposal. Fundamentally, the bullet points haven’t changed. A rebrand aligns LC State with Idaho’s four-year universities — and distinguishes LC State from the public two-year schools that have “college” in their name. University status brings LC State in line with other teaching-oriented institutions in the West. It would help LC State compete with a new wave of competition: out-of-state online schools with “university” in their title. Pemberton sees it as simple marketing. A car dealership wouldn’t want its sign to list only one make of car when it has multiple options on the lot. The same logic applies to the bloodsport of recruiting and retaining students. “It’s not a good business strategy to have a name in Idaho that implies you’re a two-year school.” LC State quickly put together a posse. (File photo courtesy of the Idaho State Department of Agriculture) Idaho state officials say they are continuing to push for full eradication of quagga mussels after again detecting the invasive species in the Snake River near Twin Falls earlier this month. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Although quagga mussels and larvae are small, state officials and conservationists say they cause giant problems because of how rapidly they reproduce. A mussel infestation can clog pipes used for irrigation and drinking water, which could have serious effects on the state’s economy, agriculture and recreation industries, officials said. “Our outlook is that not treating this infestation is not an option,” said Sydney Kennedy, a public information officer for the Idaho State Department of Agriculture said in an interview Wednesday. Gov. Brad Little agrees. Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little gives his State of the State Address from the House chambers on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “Other states have shown us what happens when invasive mussel infestations are allowed to establish before action is taken,” Little said in a written statement. “Those delayed responses have resulted in significant long-term management costs coming directly out of taxpayer pockets. Idaho has set the standard by responding aggressively. Our responsible strategy on the Snake River is proving to be effective, and we will continue making decisions that give us the best opportunity to eliminate quagga mussels to protect Idaho’s waters and the people who depend on them.” More than 1,700 different users, including municipal drinking water systems, depend on water from the Snake River, according to the state. Officials at the nonprofit Idaho Conservation League call the detection and presence of quagga mussels a no-win situation and one of the primary threats to the health of the Snake River. This month’s detection marks four consecutive years of finding quagga mussels in the Snake River near Twin Falls. In September 2023, state officials announced for the first time they had detected invasive quagga mussel larvae in water samples . Since 2023, the portion of the river where quagga mussels have been detected has shrunk, the Idaho State Department of Agriculture said. Fewer quagga mussels detected so far this year in Snake River State officials say the number of quagga mussels detected this year is down by 77% compared to last year. As of Aug. 14, the Idaho State Department of Agriculture has detected eight quagga mussel larvae, which are known as veligers, and seven adult quagga mussels. “We know what is at stake if invasive mussels gain a foothold in Idaho,” Idaho State Department of Agriculture Director Chanel Tewalt said in a written statement. “Our previous treatments have proven to be effective, and this level of containment is unprecedented among known quagga mussel infestations. items.body: U.S. District Judge B. Lynn Winmill ruled earlier this month that the state of Idaho cannot regulate abortion when a pregnancy threatens a person’s physical or mental health. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador appealed the decision, and the judge narrowed the ruling to only apply to the Boise doctor that challenged the law. (Otto Kitsinger for the Idaho Capital Sun) An Idaho federal judge has narrowed a previous ruling that had allowed abortions to protect a mother’s health or from self-harm to only apply to the Boise doctor who challenged the law. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador participates in a May 2026 roundtable at the Eisenhower Executive Office Building in Washington, D.C. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Attorney General’s Office) The narrowed ruling issued Tuesday means that Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador and the Ada County prosecutor may not enforce Idaho’s felony abortion ban in cases where Dr. Stacy Seyb administered the procedure because of serious risk of harm due to physical health or mental health concerns. Other doctors in Idaho will still be subject to Idaho’s near-total ban, which includes an exception to prevent the death of the mother but does not include exceptions to prevent her death from self-harm. Elective abortions are completely banned in Idaho. U.S. District Court of Idaho Judge B. Lynn Winmill narrowed the ruling at the request of Labrador, who argued in a recent motion that Winmill’s initial decision was too broad. Winmill agreed with Labrador, citing recent U.S. Supreme Court cases that ruled federal judges in most situations cannot issue “universal injunctions,” which block laws nationwide or more broadly than against the plaintiffs in the case. Winmill wrote “an injunction limited to Dr. Seyb will suffice to address the alleged harm.” Seyb was represented by attorneys from the Lawyering Project and Legal Voice in the case. “While we are disappointed in the ruling, it is only one step in the litigation,” Tanya Pellegrini, co-director of litigation at the Lawyering Project said in an emailed statement. “We will continue to stand with providers and their patients to ensure it is safe to be pregnant in Idaho.” Seyb is a maternal-fetal medicine physician who specializes in high-risk pregnancies. He challenged Idaho’s laws, testifying in court that he’s sent patients out of state amid health concerns because he did not feel comfortable providing abortions under the limited exceptions in Idaho’s law. Idaho’s criminal abortion ban allows an abortion to prevent the death of the mother, to treat ectopic or molar pregnancies, and in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester, if there’s been a police report filed. Doctors who provide abortions that don’t fall within those exceptions face two to five years in prison and revocation of their medical license. The judge denied Labrador’s request to fully eliminate the block on enforcement. Winmill remained “persuaded” abortions to protect women against serious health risks or against death from self-harm were constitutionally protected. Labrador on Aug. 20 also appealed Winmill’s decision to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, arguing the block defies the U.S. Supreme Court decision Dobbs v. The candidates running for a four-year term on the Boise school board offered different priorities Tuesday night during a forum at Boise High. The student-led, pro-democracy organization BABE VOTE organized the event. Election Day is Tuesday, Sept. 1. Both Hawes and Naylor are experienced attorneys with different areas of expertise. Hawes has focused on real estate and facilities as in-house corporate counsel. He works for J.R. Simplot Company and was a Boise trustee from 2021 to 2023. Naylor has experience prosecuting child protection cases and was chairman of the Governor’s Task Force on Children at Risk from 2001 to 2016. As enrollment declines, Hawes said the district needs to see facilities as assets. If the district considers closing a school, he would find creative ways to use the building to support the community. “Are there other uses that we can use for facilities that would fit squarely with what the community wants in serving students?” Hawes said. items.body: Maureen Newton waves as she uses binoculars to watch U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainees board a plane on Aug. 11, 2026, at the Magic Valley Regional Airport. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Around mid-day on a recent Tuesday in Twin Falls, a small plane landed on the tarmac at the Magic Valley Regional Airport but never taxied to the terminal. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Outside the fence surrounding the airport runway area, a group of five people watched through telescopes and binoculars as three white vans drove onto the tarmac. Around 20 men got out of the vans and boarded the plane as law enforcement oversaw the process, which took just over 30 minutes. One man was escorted back off the plane and into a van. According to a flight tracker, the plane then traveled to King County International Airport, or Boeing Field, which is located south of Seattle. Similar flights, operated by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, happen every Tuesday and Thursday at the Magic Valley airport. Shelly McDaniel and her husband Tim McDaniel record the entire boarding process for each ICE flight that operates out of the airport near Twin Falls. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Shelly McDaniel and her husband Tim McDaniel, who live about 30 minutes outside of Twin Falls, have watched every flight since they became involved in efforts to observe them on May 12. The McDaniels have recorded more than 500 detainees being flown out of the airport since flights began in early April. An ICE spokesperson told the Idaho Capital Sun the air operations provide “a network of air transportation to Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) 25 field offices to facilitate the movement of illegal aliens within the United States and their removal to destinations worldwide via air charter and commercial charter services.” “ICE is committed to the safety and welfare of those in custody throughout the entire transfer and removal process,” the spokesperson, who did not provide a name, said in an email. The spokesperson said in the Aug. 12 email that the agency had conducted 20 missions at the Magic Valley airport, also called Joslin Field. The agency’s Salt Lake City Field Office, which oversees Idaho, requests the flights “to support their operations which include the Magic Valley Region.” The Human Rights First ICE flight monitor has recorded 33 flights out of Twin Falls in 2026, and three flights out of the Boise airport. No other Idaho cities are listed. The federal immigration agency has a $1.8 billion contract with CSI Aviation, a private charter and cargo air transportation company, to operate the flights nationwide, according to federal spending data. Airport Manager Matt Barnes told the Sun in an email that the local airport does not have any formal agreement with ICE or CSI Aviation. “We are a public use airport that accepts federal grant funds, so we may not discriminate against aircraft operators who can safely operate at our facility,” Barnes said. ‘I think it’s wrong’; observers watch ICE flights because of due process concerns. Idaho lawmaker says operations enforce ‘rule of law’ Maureen Newton, left, and Karen Stroder, observe an ICE flight on Aug. 11, 2026, out of the Magic Valley Regional Airport. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Karen Stroder has lived in Twin Falls nearly 30 years and in Idaho her entire life, she said. She got involved in watching the ICE flights through a local chapter of the group Indivisible, a progressive advocacy organization. “I think it’s wrong,” Stroder said of the flights. “I don’t think people are getting due process. I think everybody deserves their day in court.” Twin Falls resident Heather Muth, who helped found the local Indivisible group, learned from an Indiana chapter member that these flights were happening and that various groups tracked and recorded them. items.body: Middleton School District trustees approved a name and tabled construction bids for the new elementary school at a special Tuesday afternoon meeting. The board tabled voting on a bid package for the new elementary school’s construction because potential bidders were not able to prepare bids in time. It will meet again next week to vote. The new Freedom Elementary, a name voted on by district constituents, won’t be far — in nomenclature or distance — from Independence Elementary, a new elementary school on the West Ada School District side of Star. Middleton’s new elementary will be located on the Canyon County side of Star, a city in two counties. It will serve one of the state’s fastest-growing areas and alleviate overcrowding in two elementary schools. In other action, trustees approved language for a $3 million supplemental levy, spread over two years, to fund teaching and classified positions, new curriculum, school resource officers, classroom technology and a “hot topic:” extracurricular transportation. The deadline for districts to submit ballot language is Friday, Aug. 28. After a failed supplemental levy in May, Middleton administrators made a round of cuts to staff, curricula and logistics. Constituents have been particularly frustrated by the lack of busing for extracurricular activities like sports, trustees said. Superintendent Marc Gee also presented language for a $2.8 million levy, an increase of about $2 per year per $100,000 of property value to taxpayers, over the $3 million option. Trustees didn’t like it. “I would say two dollars makes a big difference when it comes to taking care of our schools that we’re jamming full,” Dempsey said in favor of running the larger $3 million levy. Trustee Jay Clark suggested putting the transportation issue front-and-center in the levy. “That should give us some more votes, if that’s a hot topic,” Clark said. Trustees also approved a list of potential mascots for the new school: Elementary students will vote to choose between being Eagles, Falcons, Pioneers, Patriots or Stars. The board has not yet scheduled a special meeting for next week when it will decide on a bid package for Freedom Elementary’s construction. items.body: Gov. Brad Little, center, tosses dirt with a shovel next to Idaho State Police Col. Bill Gardiner, right, at a groundbreaking ceremony for a new forensics laboratory on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Correction: This story was updated at 7:30 p.m. due to incorrect information shared by Idaho State Police about the funding source for the new facility. The forensics lab’s construction is funded through state general funds appropriated in 2022 through House Bill 779. State law enforcement officials broke ground Tuesday on a new forensics laboratory that they hope will improve the state’s already-fast processing of criminal forensics evidence. And they hope that the $29 million forensics laboratory , based at Idaho State Police’s Headquarters in Meridian, will streamline lab services that are tapped by local and county law enforcement agencies across the state. Moments before officials ceremonially lifted dirt with shovels, Gov. Brad Little talked about the need for the facility in a state that has grown at a record pace in recent years. “The people that have been here expect a safe environment. And you can’t have effective law enforcement if you don’t have the tools that they need to do their job,” Little said. Officials expect construction on the lab to finish in January 2028. The new facility will help aid DNA testing, including advancements to establish Whole Genome Sequencing; examining latent prints; forensics for digital devices; and house technology to help solve gun-related crimes through the National Integrated Ballistic Information Network, officials say. Idaho State Police’s director, Col. items.body: Firefighters on the Claremont Fire in Boise, Idaho on July 6, 2026. Drought across the Northwest has exacerbated wildfire conditions in the region. (Photo by Brenen Helgerson/ National Interagency Fire Center) The last weeks of summer find Oregon and much of the Northwest experiencing historic drought, exacerbating what has become one of the most active wildfire seasons in the state and region, according to state and federal climatologists and hydrologists. Beyond fish and ecological impacts, drought across Oregon, Idaho and Washington is causing water supply shortages for public water and electric utilities, costing farmers tens of millions of dollars in lost crops and leaving vegetation and soils dry and susceptible to fires. Wildfire and drought maps overlaid by Oregon’s State Climatologist Larry O’Neill on Monday during an online drought and climate outlook meeting hosted by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration show the summer’s wildfires popping up over historically dry areas of the state and region. About 4% of Oregon’s total land area — 2.4 million acres of mostly rangeland — has burned in the current fire season, most of which occurred within a one-month period. Overall, about 3.5 million acres have burned across the Northwest, including fires in and around Spokane that became some of the most destructive in Washington history. “Drought didn’t cause these ignitions, but they created the conditions with exceptionally dry vegetation and fuels that favor rapid fire growth and extreme impacts once those fires started,” O’Neill said. He and Catherine Fitzpatrick, a hydrologist at NOAA’s Northwest River Forecast Center, detailed water levels and conditions in the Northwest’s rivers, reservoirs and snowpack for a 90-day period, as well as the impacts of temperature anomalies. Even with a potential deluge of precipitation this winter in what O’Neill expects to be a “very strong” or “super” El Niño weather pattern, water reservoirs in the region are so depleted that there’s unlikely to be much carryover in water supplies into next year, the two warned. “Across the Pacific Northwest we’re substantially depleting our reservoir storage, and now we’re getting into kind of the later part of August and September, and reservoirs are being emptied out,” O’Neill said. “There’s little hope for carryover into the next water year, and then as I mentioned earlier, we’re seeing record low stream flows occurring in all three states.” Anomalous heat Most of eastern Oregon and southern Idaho have experienced summer temperatures 2 to 4 degrees Fahrenheit above normal, following what was the warmest fall and winter on record for the entire region, where temperatures in Oregon and Idaho were 3 to 5 degrees Fahrenheit above normal. Most of Oregon east of the Cascades has in the last 90 days experienced “extreme drought,” a NOAA designation indicating major crop and pasture losses, and widespread water shortages or restrictions. About 4% of Oregon in and around Grant, Baker and Wheeler counties in the eastern part of the state are in what NOAA classifies as “exceptional drought,” meaning it reached historic levels, among other indicators. It’s the second time since 2000 that Grant County has received the designation. Despite being surrounded by the Blue Mountains, the area saw the lowest snowpack on record this winter. About 8% of Idaho is experiencing exceptional drought, particularly in Owyhee, Twin Falls and Cassia counties in southern Idaho. Cuts to irrigation water supply for Idaho farmers have cost them $20 million so far according to crop insurance indemnities that are being paid out, O’Neill said, but the total cost is likely to be far higher as many claims won’t be processed until after the growing season ends. In the Yakima Basin in Washington, water users are receiving about 58% of their allotment. That includes the Roza Irrigation district, which supports more than $1.5 billion in annual agricultural revenue for the state.

As of August 2026, the commission authorized 67 schools, including four that have yet to open. Seven were virtual. There are 85 charter schools in the state, meaning the commission authorizes 79% of Idaho charters. The rest are authorized by school districts. What does the commission do? The commission authorizes and oversees most charter schools in the state. This includes authorizing schools to open and monitoring their financial, operational and academic success. How does the commission authorize a new school? The authorization process starts when a group hoping to found a new school contacts charter commission staff. Typically, that group includes the school’s founding board, which must establish a nonprofit corporation and establish 501(c)(3) status to apply. People interested in founding a charter school can take the Idaho Department of Education’s Charter 101 course. The founding group works with commission staff to submit an application packet that includes financial planning, school model information and evidence of student demand. The group then presents to the full commission, which can vote to authorize or deny the application. The commission has only denied a handful of applications over the last two decades, at least two received approval at a later date. Before opening, schools have a series of conditions to meet and have monthly meetings with commission staff to work toward completing pre-opening steps. The school’s governing board operates the school independently under its charter, subject to commission oversight. Schools are initially authorized for six years under a traditional charter. Schools authorized under the 2024 innovative charter law are authorized for three years. The commission meets every other month, typically in Boise. How does the commission hold existing schools accountable? The commission has standards that schools must meet related to finances, test scores and graduation rates, among other things. If a school meets those requirements, they continue operating with little commission interaction for their term. Schools that fail to meet a condition typically have a year to meet the metric. If they don’t, the commission can start proceedings to revoke the schools charter. However, a revocation has happened twice. Odyssey Charter School closed in 2015 and Nampa Classical Charter School closed in 2010, both shortly after opening. Another Choice, a virtual school, had its charter non-renewed in 2022 and was subsequently forced to close. Schools in good standing with the commission can have their charter renewed for 12 years if they meet certain criteria. Renewals can also be for a six year term. Who serves on the commission? The commission is made up of seven members appointed by the Governor. Commission staff handles the day-to-day work of supporting the commission and helping with charter oversight. Who makes up the commission staff? The commission faced significant staff turnover in recent years. Rachel Burk was hired in August 2025 as executive director. She filled a series of staff vacancies. The commission currently has two program managers, a finance program manager and an administrative assistant on staff. What is the charter commission’s annual budget? (Photo by Allison Joyce/Getty Images) WASHINGTON — With just over two months until the November midterms, the U.S. Supreme Court gave way Monday for President Donald Trump to have a hand in regulating mail-in ballots nationwide, a voting method he has falsely claimed is rife with corruption since he lost the 2020 presidential election. In an unsigned emergency docket opinion , the court’s conservative majority wrote the Trump administration is likely to prevail on its argument that 23 Democratic-led states do not have standing to stop his executive order to change how the U.S. Postal Service processes mail-in ballots. The majority justices also wrote that a lower court’s injunction is “causing irreparable harm,” but left open the possibility that the executive order could still be considered unconstitutional. “The Court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell,” the majority wrote. The legality of a Massachusetts federal district court order, which paused the executive order to overhaul vote-by-mail systems before the Nov. 3 midterms, will now be decided by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit. Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented. In a lengthy dissent, Jackson wrote the ruling “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections.” The principle of courts not altering voting systems too close to the election has been eroded, she said, amounting to a “Kafkaesque nightmare.” “States administering elections and the voting public that relies on them to do so deserve clarity, not caginess or confusion,” she wrote. Final rule issued The March 31 executive order at the heart of the case in part directs USPS to direct the redesign of mail-in ballot envelopes, including adding a unique barcode. It also asks USPS to collect voters’ names and addresses from state elections officials and directs the U.S. Justice Department to investigate and prosecute state officials who violate the order. The Postal Service issued a final rule Friday detailing how the process would be carried out. Whether an overhaul of mail-in ballots for each state could be completed in time for the Nov. 3 election remains to be seen, as vote-by-mail documents are sent to voters well in advance of Election Day. A federal district judge in Massachusetts chastised the Trump administration for sowing confusion and “creating” an emergency by noticing a rule Friday that the U.S. Postal Service will eventually require federally regulated mail-in ballot voting envelopes and state data. A 95-page notice alerting that the final rule would appear in the Federal Register on Aug. 26 outlined justifications for federal requirements on states to redesign ballot envelopes and provide a list of recipient names and addresses to USPS. The final rule became effective Friday, according to the document. items.body: Update Monday with news that Crestpoint is “winding down” its relationship with Smarter By 1 Degree. Students at Eagle-based private school Freedom Academy can pursue a bachelor’s degree before they graduate high school. The path runs through Texas-based company Smarter By 1 Degree, which connects high schoolers with online college courses and participating universities. Many Idaho public high schoolers already earn some college credit and even associate degrees , but Smarter By 1 Degree says its students can earn a bachelor’s degree alongside their high school diploma by taking online courses at “partner” universities. The company touts its compatibility with a dozen private school choice programs. Becky Butlin, a Freedom Academy administrator who oversees high school students, said she was researching homeschool coursework last year when she came across the program. Smarter By 1 Degree seemed “a little sketchy” at first, Butlin said, but she later spoke with representatives from the company and parents whose children graduated from the bachelor’s degree program. “That’s where I became more comfortable and said, ‘Oh no, this is a real thing.’ It’s a good curriculum, solid curriculum, and … has that partnership with the universities.” Some of those university relationships appear tenuous, however. When Idaho Education News reached out to the institutions that offer courses through the program, one president denied having a “partnership” with the company — and threatened to sue EdNews if it described the arrangement that way. Smarter By 1 Degree subsequently removed its university partners from its website and asked EdNews not to name them. “These partnerships are important business and academic relationships, and we have intentionally chosen not to publicly identify certain university partners,” Chloe Whiteford, the CEO’s assistant, said by email . “Publishing information that was provided to you directly during a conversation … could negatively affect those partnerships.” Freedom Academy partnered with Smarter By 1 Degree last year. About 20 students are enrolled in its high school, and enrollment grows each year, administrators said. One student is scheduled to graduate in 2028 with a business administration degree from Crestpoint University. Who’s who? Freedom Academy: A private, for-profit nondenominational Christian school in Eagle. Started in 2022, it integrates lessons about faith and the Socratic method into its pedagogy. Freedom Academy began using Smarter By 1 Degree about a year ago with a small cohort of high school students. Smarter By 1 Degree: A Texas-based alternative learning company and online private school primarily serving homeschool families. Smarter By 1 Degree has students in every state and a handful of other countries. Crestpoint University: A private, online university based in Arizona. It offers coursework and degrees to students it receives from Smarter By 1 Degree, but it denies any sort of partnership with Smarter By 1 Degree. The university is formerly known as National Paralegal College. Mixing faith-based learning with higher education Ashley Meyer, the K-12 school’s founder, built Freedom Academy based on what she experienced in her spiritual life after leaving home. Unable to answer questions about her faith, she walked away from the Catholic Church she was raised in. Now a nondenominational Protestant, Meyer’s goal is to equip Freedom Academy students with the ability to endure questioning and remain faithful. The Socratic method is baked into Freedom Academy instruction to make critical thinking and learning natural for students. Teachers and administrators weave Bible lessons into the coursework. “Faith is woven into everything we do, so you can’t escape it,” Meyer said of Freedom Academy. items.body: This month, taxpayers in Texas found out how many students receiving $1 billion in private education subsidies were already homeschooled or enrolled in a private school: 70%. Taxpayers in Idaho are still waiting to get that number from a similar private school choice program that serves nearly nine and a half times fewer students, costs $950 million less and was enacted two months earlier. And it’s not for lack of trying. Between February and July, the Idaho State Tax Commission received seven public records requests related to the Parental Choice Tax Credit. A college faculty member, a hobbyist data analyst, a homeschool advocate, a former public school superintendent and two journalists filed requests seeking data that would shed light on who’s benefitting from the $50 million-a-year taxpayer-funded program. Four of those requests — including two from Idaho Education News — sought the number of tax-credit recipients who previously attended a public school. This data would test a selling point of the program: that it helps students who couldn’t otherwise afford a private education. That tally doesn’t include unofficial requests. Democratic lawmakers, who asked for data in March, weren’t included in a tracking sheet of records requests obtained by EdNews. Nearly all of the requests were denied. items.body: Idaho Power serves more than 660,000 customers across Idaho and Oregon. The Boise-based utility is looking to sell its Oregon service territory, which represents 4% of its customers, to the Oregon Trail Electric Cooperative for $154 million by early 2027. (Courtesy of Idaho Power) Idaho’s largest utility is seeking a $154 million transfer of all of its Oregon service territory to a locally-owned utility based in Baker City. Idaho Power is awaiting approval from state and federal regulators to sell its Oregon service territory to the Oregon Trail Electric Cooperative, which serves 60,000 customers in John Day, Burns and La Grande across 6,700 square miles. If the sale is approved, the transfer would add 20,000 former Idaho Power customers to the utility’s grid across 4,700 square miles in Malheur, Harney, Baker and Wallowa counties. Idaho Power has served Eastern Oregon customers for more than a century, with those customers representing 4% of the company’s business. Selling its Oregon service territory would allow the company to keep rates affordable for customers as the utility experiences an unprecedented energy demand , according to the company’s application to the Idaho Public Utilities Commission. The sale will not change any of Idaho Power’s customer rates, but new Oregon Trail Electric Cooperative customers will likely see a 5.7% increase to their rates to make up for the cost of the investment, according to the utility. Without the sale, Idaho Power would have needed to raise its general rate for Oregon customers by at least 17% to compensate for the costs of new company investments and inflation. The Oregon Trail Electric Cooperative will buy nearly all of Idaho Power’s distribution lines, substations and equipment located in Oregon. While Idaho Power would no longer serve Oregon retail electric customers, it would continue to own and operate some generation and transmission resources located in Oregon such the Boardman to Hemingway transmission line, which provides power to Idaho, Oregon and across the region. The transfer is expected to close in early 2027. items.body: Idaho has yet another growing education gap: a CTE chasm. Yes, career-technical education is booming. But it’s growing unevenly. In bigger districts, and in areas like the Treasure Valley, students have more options, more opportunities. In small towns, CTE offerings are limited. And that affects rural students and communities alike. A new state report puts Idaho’s urban-rural CTE gap into sharp focus. Providing additional programs — and pushing these programs into small-town Idaho — won’t be easy. And it won’t be cheap, either. Peter Risse " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Peter-Risse-943x1180.webp" class="wp-image-108603" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Peter-Risse-496x620.webp" alt="" width="300" height="375" srcset="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Peter-Risse-496x620.webp 496w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Peter-Risse-943x1180.webp 943w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Peter-Risse-160x200.webp 160w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Peter-Risse.webp 1152w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 300px) 100vw, 300px" /> Peter Risse During a recent legislative hearing , Division of Career Technical Education administrator Peter Risse didn’t sugarcoat the situation. “A student’s ZIP code should not limit their access to the education and training needed to support a successful career in the community of their choice.” The trouble is, that’s exactly what is happening right now. And the report from the state’s Office of Performance Evaluations proved it. The OPE, the Legislature’s research arm, looked at the scope of Idaho’s 1,103 secondary career-technical programs — to see what is offered, and where. About 40% of the state’s CTE programs are clustered in what researchers called “city” schools — a mere 15 of the 125 districts and charters that offer CTE programs. Smaller districts and charters offer a limited CTE menu, mostly in agriculture, business and marketing. “(They) are not offering a smaller version of the same CTE programs found in larger districts and urban areas,” according to the report , released Aug. 7. “They are offering a narrower set of options concentrated in the program areas that require the least specialized facilities and equipment.” Conversely — and of acute concern in a state facing acute rural healthcare shortages — CTE programs in health professions are almost nonexistent in small-town schools. Idaho’s “city” schools, those 15 districts and charters, offer 63 of Idaho’s 98 CTE programs in healthcare fields: a whopping 64% of the total. “(It) really depends on where you’re going to school and where you live,” Casey Petti, the OPE’s principal evaluator, told lawmakers. Responding to an OPE survey, school officials said their students and local employers most needed training in ag, food and natural resources — no surprise, especially in rural communities. For one thing, instructors in ag and natural resource programs command lower salaries than their CTE colleagues in engineering or health professions. In the OPE survey, 68% of district and charter officials said they would like to add career-technical programs, but can’t. And 54% of respondents said they wanted to add offerings in health professions or public safety; 21% specifically listed nursing assistant programs as an area of need. items.body: Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador speaks at a press conference outside the U.S. Supreme Court on April 24, 2024, in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images) Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador announced Thursday his office is appealing a recent federal court ruling allowing abortions to protect the mother’s health or prevent her death from self-harm. Labrador is asking a federal appeals court to block the decision, allowing the near-total abortion ban to be enforced as written. Idaho judge ruling allows abortion if it protects mother’s health, prevents self-harm Labrador argued that U.S. District of Idaho Judge B. Lynn Winmill’s ruling defied the U.S. Supreme Court decision Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health, which overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, according to a press release from Labrador’s office. The legal battle stems from a lawsuit from Dr. Stacy Seyb , a Boise maternal-fetal medicine specialist, who argued that Idaho’s abortion bans were unconstitutional because they didn’t allow abortions to protect a mother’s health, her future fertility or if her mental health put her at risk of self-harm. Labrador said Winmill’s ruling “has replaced Idaho’s law with his own abortion standard,” and that Idaho’s law does allow for pregnant patients with medical emergencies to be treated in the state. “Dobbs made clear that abortion policy belongs to the people and their elected state representatives, not the judiciary,” Labrador said in a press release . “We have appealed to the Ninth Circuit, and we will fight until this ruling is reversed and Idaho’s law is restored.” Seyb is represented by attorneys from the Lawyering Project and Legal Voice. “The Attorney General’s utter disregard for the health and welfare of pregnant Idaho residents is appalling,” Stephanie Toti, executive director of the Lawyering Project, said in an email. “We look forward to continuing to litigate this case with the goal of making it safer for people to be pregnant in Idaho.” Idaho’s criminal abortion ban allows abortion to prevent the death of the mother, to treat ectopic or molar pregnancies, and in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester, if there’s been a police report filed. Doctors who provide abortions that don’t fall within those exceptions face two to five years in prison and revocation of their medical license. Idaho also has a civil-enforcement ban on abortion, allowing family members to sue abortion providers for a minimum of $20,000 if an abortion occurs after six weeks or after fetal heartbeat activity is detected. Winmill’s 81-page decision said the U.S. Constitution protects access to abortion in certain high-risk cases that went beyond the exemptions outlined in Idaho’s ban. A voter-led initiative will appear on November ballots this year that, if approved, would overturn Idaho’s abortion ban and enumerate protections to women’s reproductive healthcare and privacy into law. Labrador’s appeal also argues that Winmill’s decision should not be applied to every doctor in the state, but only Seyb because he is the one who challenged the law. He said the Winmill’s decision violates the 2025 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that said federal courts cannot in most cases issue “universal injunctions,” which broadly block enforcement of laws for everyone, not just the parties to the lawsuit. items.body: Members of the Idaho Legislature's Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee and their staff tour Southwest Idaho Treatment Center, or SWITC, in Nampa on Nov. 20, 2024. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun) People with disabilities are hearing the words ‘institutionalization’ and ‘Olmstead’ daily. This shift in the way policymakers openly discuss the segregation of people with disabilities naturally follows nationwide budget cuts to home and community-based services. If people with disabilities cannot get the services and supports they need to live independently in their homes and communities, where are they to go? As an Idaho historian and a person with a disability, it is clear to me that whether or not you or a member of your family has personally experienced disability, whether or not you have a friend or colleague who is disabled, or you work in the field of direct care for people with disabilities, everyone should be paying attention to the evolving language of institutionalization. Idaho has a long history with institutionalization and a shift back to overreliance on this practice by either federal or state policymakers presents the same constitutional and moral danger. As federal protections fade, Americans with disabilities fear a return to institutions Idaho statehood and the institutionalization of people with disabilities were entwined. The state of Idaho wasted no time getting into the business of institutionalizing people with disabilities whether those disabilities were intellectual or developmental, mental illness, verbal or non-verbal, in adults or adolescents. People with physical disabilities were not always immune from the practice. The question of whether these Idahoans were better suited for living independently in their communities with appropriate supports wouldn’t be asked for nearly a century. The Idaho Insane Asylum, the original name for what is now State Hospital South, was established in 1886, four years prior to Idaho statehood. It had an original capacity of 300 beds. In 1889 at the state constitutional convention, language was included to formally establish the hospital in Blackfoot. Idaho’s founders decided that institutionalizing people with disabilities was the only way to deal with the scourge of difference. Families were encouraged to lock away their family members with disabilities, and many did exactly that. As the state grew, so did its institutions. The Northern Idaho Sanitarium at Orofino, now State Hospital North, would follow in 1905 with a 250-bed capacity. The Idaho Sanitarium for the Feeble-minded and Epileptic came in 1911 with an original capacity of 250 beds primarily for adolescent “inmates,” a term that was used for far too long in referring to Idahoans with disabilities residing in our state hospitals. It has had an array of names including the State School and Colony for the Feeble-minded, Idaho State School and Hospital and now the Southwestern Idaho Treatment Center. As slippery slope arguments go, the day the state opened these institutions was a slippery slope toward an expensive and morally dubious enterprise. While the state’s population grew, the population of these hospitals exploded. In the 1930s to 1950s, the population to capacity issue abounded at each of the hospitals. By 1955, 1,221 Idahoans were institutionalized by the state in hospitals rife with overcrowding, abuse, neglect and doctor to patient ratios that are horrifying by today’s standards. In 1970, a report found the adolescent residents of the Idaho State School and Hospital to be living in substandard conditions. It was the independent living movement that forced the question of whether institutionalization was constitutional and if it was the best way to care for people with disabilities who had been locked away from society since the 19 th century. items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on March 16, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho state budget officials have an improved revenue outlook for the new fiscal year in a forecast released Monday. The Division of Financial Management revised its revenue forecast for Fiscal Year 2027, which began July1. The new forecast is just over $291.1 million, or 5.2% higher than what legislative budget writers predicted, according to the July Revenue Monitor report. Home July, the first month of the current fiscal year, saw state revenues come in $13.1 million above the new forecast. Individual income tax, sales tax and miscellaneous revenue all came in above the forecast. Corporate income tax collections were $15.9 million lower than projected, according to the report. Overall, July revenue was $5.6 million lower than the previous year, the report said. “If monthly revenue collections follow the new forecast exactly for the remainder of the year, the new projected ending balance is $619.5 million,” the report said. State agencies will submit their budget requests for next year at the beginning of September, and legislators will consider the requests during the 2027 legislative session. Lawmakers will convene in January at the Capitol for the session. Idaho Division of Financial Management Administrator Lori Wolff gives a press briefing prior to Gov. Brad Little’s State of the State address on Jan. 12, 2026, in the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee room at the Capitol in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) The revised forecast comes after state budget officials announced it ended the 2026 fiscal year with a positive cash balance, the Idaho Capital Sun reported. Brad Little named an Idaho Supreme Court justice to fill a vacancy left by the retiring chief justice. Little appointed Fourth District Judge Jason Scott to fill outgoing Chief Justice Richard Bevan’s seat on the state’s highest court, the governor’s office announced Tuesday. Scott is an Idaho native who earned an accounting degree at Idaho State University before graduating from Duke University’s School of Law in 1997. After law school, he returned to Idaho — clerking for a U.S. district judge and working for 15 years at the law firm Hawley Troxell, including seven years as a partner at the firm. His legal practice focused on civil litigation. Justice Robyn Brody to become chief justice of Idaho Supreme Court “Judge Scott has dedicated his career to the law and to serving the people of Idaho,” Little said in a written statement. “His experience as a practicing attorney and a district judge gives him a strong understanding of both the courtroom and the broader legal system. I am confident he will bring thoughtful judgment, a strong work ethic, and a deep commitment to the rule of law to the Idaho Supreme Court.” In 2014, Scott was first appointed as a district judge in Idaho’s Fourth Judicial District, which includes Ada County. As a judge, he has presided over high-stakes lawsuits — including a legal challenge to the state’s strict abortion ban and an open meetings lawsuit over University of Idaho’s attempted purchase of the University of Phoenix . He also serves as presiding district judge in Valley County. “For twelve years, I’ve given my all to serving the people of Idaho as a district judge,” Scott said in a written statement. “I’m grateful to Governor Little for entrusting me with the opportunity to continue in public service as a justice of the Idaho Supreme Court. I will always perform the duties of the office to the best of my ability, and I look forward to collaborating with my new colleagues on the Court to decide cases with the utmost care and fidelity to the law.” Scott is set to fill the seat upon Bevan’s retirement on Oct. 30. Weisman/Rhode Island Current) In the summer of 2023, a third of the fire engines owned
items.body: A decades-old pumper truck owned by the Providence Fire Department in Rhode Island, where it’s used for events and ceremonies. Providence is one of dozens of cities accusing fire truck manufacturers of conspiring to suppress the supply of trucks, raising prices and driving up delivery times. (Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current) In the summer of 2023, a third of the fire engines owned by the fire department in Kansas City, Kansas, were unusable. Five of 15 pumper trucks were out of commission, and the department was waiting on parts from the manufacturer. So Kansas City fire officials went on a nationwide hunt for trucks. But their frantic search turned up just four they could buy immediately, and the vehicles were designed for smaller, more rural departments. Their experience was not unusual: Municipalities and fire departments in every state are struggling with soaring prices and years-long delivery times for trucks. It’s a crisis many cities and departments lay squarely at the feet of the country’s biggest fire apparatus manufacturers. “There must come a day of reckoning when the manufacturers of our most important tools are held accountable for runaway pricing and extended delivery times,” Dennis Rubin, the chief of the Kansas City Fire Department, told U.S. senators last fall at hearing convened to investigate price increases and delivery delays on fire trucks. Kansas City is one of more than 60 cities, counties and fire departments across the nation — from Milwaukee to San Diego, Pittsburgh to Tampa — that say the country’s three biggest fire truck manufacturers have conspired to suppress competition, resulting in skyrocketing prices for fire trucks and repair parts, and yearslong manufacturing delays. In April, a federal court rolled up their claims into a trio of antitrust class action lawsuits in a Wisconsin district court. The defendants are fire apparatus manufacturers REV Group Inc., Oshkosh Corporation and Rosenbauer Group, along with some of their subsidiaries and related companies, as well as their trade group, the Fire Apparatus Manufacturers’ Association. Des Moines sues fire truck companies, alleging ‘parasitic’ pricing, anti-trust violations By some estimates , the three manufacturers together control 70-80% of the U.S. fire truck market. Fire engine prices have nearly doubled since 2020 , from about $589,000 to over $1 million, according to the International Association of Fire Fighters. Fire departments also are reporting extended wait times for new fire trucks. In 2024, officials with the Seattle Fire Department noted it took more than four years to replace a ladder truck — a process that had previously taken just a year. And some departments are accusing manufacturers of charging them “floating prices” that increase soon before a truck is ready to be delivered. The president of a volunteer fire department in Delaware County, Pennsylvania, said his department paid a 50% deposit on a fire truck and the supplier later said it could no longer deliver at that price, leading to the department paying an additional $110,000, reported the Pennsylvania Capital-Star. “By hiking prices for trucks and replacement parts without competition, the defendants have made it harder for the city of Pittsburgh and other municipalities across the country to make the required investments in lifesaving services and put the burden back on our communities,” Pittsburgh Mayor Corey O’Connor said in a July statement announcing its antitrust lawsuit. A city representative declined to comment further. The plaintiffs in the suit assert that manufacturers worked together to throttle the production of fire trucks nationwide and minimize competition to increase prices. Many cities and fire departments also allege the Fire Apparatus Manufacturers’ Association — the industry’s primary trade group — helped the manufacturers coordinate price increases and limit production by passing secret or proprietary data between them. New research suggests that mice, not deer, are closely linked to increases in young ticks, while large acorn crops can help predict higher tick numbers two years later. (Photo courtesy of Robin Moore/Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies) For more than three decades, researchers have been tracking ticks, mice, oak trees and other wildlife in a New York forest to better understand what makes Lyme disease more likely to spread. Their latest findings challenge some long-held assumptions — including the idea that deer are a major driver of Lyme disease risk. Researchers at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies, a nonprofit environmental research group, found that white-footed mice, not white-tailed deer, are closely linked to the number of young blacklegged ticks, the life stage most likely to infect people with Lyme disease. A year with a large mouse population was followed by about a 40% increase in nymphal ticks the following year. But more mice don’t necessarily mean a higher percentage of ticks carrying Lyme bacteria. Researchers initially expected the two to rise together because white-footed mice are especially good at transmitting the bacteria to ticks. The researchers found that other animals, including skunks, squirrels and opossums, also feed larval ticks. Because those animals are less efficient at transmitting the bacteria, the mix of hosts can affect how many ticks become infected. In other words, mouse populations can help predict how many ticks there will be, but not necessarily how many will carry Lyme bacteria. The researchers also found that large crops of acorns can set off a chain reaction: More acorns mean more food for mice, which can mean more ticks two years later. The findings come as tick-borne diseases are an increasing public health concern. Lyme disease is the most commonly reported tick-borne disease in the United States, with nearly half a million people diagnosed each year, according to the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The study, published in the peer-reviewed Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences journal, draws on data collected since 1991 at a 2,000-acre research site in Dutchess County, New York. The researchers also found that extreme heat and cold don’t necessarily kill blacklegged ticks in the wild. The ticks appear able to shelter in soil and leaf litter during extreme temperatures. The team plans to continue monitoring how ticks, wildlife, trees and climate interact — and what those changes could mean for human health, according to a news release. This new research comes as scientists and public health officials are also watching ticks expand into new parts of the country. Lone star ticks, once primarily associated with the Southeast, are now established across much of the South, Midwest and Northeast. An adult female is distinguished by a white dot or “lone star” on her back. The ticks can transmit several diseases and are associated with alpha-gal syndrome, an allergy to a molecule found in red meat and other products from mammals. As lone star tick populations have spread, more states are paying attention to alpha-gal syndrome, which experts believe is significantly underdiagnosed. Massachusetts, Missouri and Oklahoma have expanded surveillance or public education efforts in recent years, and all three have joined the growing list of states that require alpha-gal syndrome to be reported to public health officials. At least 14 states have added or will soon add alpha-gal syndrome to their lists of reportable diseases, according to the Alpha-gal Alliance Action Fund, a nonprofit advocacy group. In those states, health care providers and laboratories must report cases to state health departments. Lawmakers in Ohio also are considering a similar measure that would make alpha-gal syndrome a reportable disease. The bill has passed the House and remains under consideration in the Senate. items.body: West Nile virus is present each year across Southeast Idaho. (Courtesy of Pixabay) A Canyon County resident over the age of 65 is Idaho’s first reported human case of West Nile virus meningitis this year, public health officials announced Monday. The infected person was hospitalized but is recovering at home, the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare announced in a news release . Infected mosquitoes spread West Nile virus through bites. Idaho health officials pointed to the case of the disease to encourage people to take steps to prevent mosquito bites while outdoors and on their properties. “The report of the first severe West Nile virus disease of the season in an Idaho resident is a good reminder for all of us to take protective measures against mosquito bites,” Idaho State Epidemiologist Dr. Christine Hahn said in a written statement. “This includes wearing insect repellent and protective clothing in addition to reducing standing water around gardens and homes where mosquitoes can lay eggs.” Most people infected with West Nile don’t feel sick. A fifth of people infected develop a fever and other symptoms like a headache, body aches, joint pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, swollen lymph glands or a rash. Risk of severe illness, and death, can be up to 40% higher in people that take immune system suppressants, such as treatments for cancer, autoimmune disease, and organ transplants, said Southwest District Health Epidemiologist Lekshmi Rita Venugopal. “With West Nile virus detected in mosquitoes in Southwest Idaho again this summer, it’s especially important for people with weakened immune systems to avoid mosquito bites,” she said in a written statement. The risk of severe illness is higher for older people and people who have some medical conditions. Severe illness can affect the brain and spinal cord, and can lead to hospitalization or death. Officials encourage people who believe they are sick with West Nile to contact their healthcare provider. Tips to avoid West Nile virus To avoid West Nile infections, Health and Welfare encourages people to: Avoid mosquitoes, especially when those that spread West Nile virus are most active between dusk and dawn. When outdoors, wear loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and pants. Use insect repellents on exposed skin. Find repellents approved by the Environmental Protection Agency, or EPA, and follow product instructions carefully. Find repellents online using the EPA’s search tool or a CDC chatbot . Use mosquito netting to cover strollers and baby carriers. People should also take steps to mitigate mosquitos on their property, Health and Welfare suggests, including: If your home has damaged screens, repair or replace them. Mosquitos like to breed in standing water. Reduce standing water on your property, including toys, trays or pots outdoors that can hold water. For bird baths, static decorative ponds and animal water tanks, change water weekly to prevent mosquito larvae from maturing into adults. Find more tips online on Health and Welfare’s website . items.body: A mother and her son hold hands on a swing set. This year, more state and local leaders are pushing to hold parents accountable for their children’s behavior, particularly when it involves serious criminal offenses. (Photo by Troy Bennett/Maine Morning Star) When young children and teenagers get into trouble, the question often comes quickly: Where were their parents? That question is again shaping public policy in communities across the country, as state and local lawmakers and prosecutors increasingly look for ways to respond to concerns about youth crime and public disorder. Some proposals would strengthen enforcement of existing laws that allow parents to be fined or otherwise held responsible for their children’s conduct. Others would impose youth curfews or establish new requirements for parents to perform community service or pay fines — measures considered in places such as Albany County, New York; Chicago; and Columbus, Ohio. But experts note there’s little proof the laws work. A new law in Louisiana, which went into effect earlier this month, allows courts to fine parents or guardians up to $5,000 if a youth age 14 or older is convicted of making a school threat. State lawmakers also recently requested a study on the link between parenting, discipline and juvenile delinquency. Louisiana already has one of the nation’s toughest laws, allowing parents to be prosecuted when their child under 17 is involved in a violent felony, with penalties of up to 10 years in prison. A new law in New Jersey that went into effect earlier this year makes parents liable when their child incites a public brawl that causes property damage. Parents of children who commit the most serious offenses could face up to six months in jail and a $1,000 fine. Parents and guardians can have enormous influence over the children in their care, some proponents argue, so holding them accountable could give them another incentive to keep their children in school, enforce rules and steer them away from crime. Every state has some form of parental responsibility law. But there is little empirical evidence showing that the laws actually reduce youth crime. “We just don’t know,” said Eve Brank, a psychology professor at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln. Brank has spent decades studying the implementation and effectiveness of those laws, and said there have not been any gold-standard empirical research studies on the subject. Her research also suggests that these laws are not commonly enforced. The renewed interest is also playing out in Washington, D.C., where U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro announced in May that district parents may face up to six months in jail if they knowingly allow their children to commit crimes. The move came in response to “teen takeovers,” or large, unruly gatherings of teens. The day after Pirro announced the policy change, a group of teenagers got into a violent brawl at a Chipotle in the Navy Yard neighborhood. Video of the fight quickly spread online, and Pirro later used the incident to underscore her warning to parents. “We’re looking at the parents to make sure that they understand that they are responsible for the upheaval that is going on,” Pirro said at a news conference. The idea of holding parents responsible for their children’s criminal behavior has resurfaced repeatedly over the past several decades, often during periods when public concern about youth crime is high. By 1995, more than 40 states had enacted some form of parental responsibility law, according to a 2000 research article published in The Social Science Journal. The laws varied widely, from requiring parents to attend counseling or parenting classes to imposing fines and, in some cases, imprisonment.
