items.body: (UPDATED, 6:32 p.m., with details on Zak’s salary.) New Boise State University president David Hahn has created a new top management post — and hired a former colleague to fill it. Mitch Zak Hahn has hired Mitch Zak as Boise State’s new chief public and external affairs officer. In an email to the campus community, Hahn said he decided to “repurpose” a vacant leadership position to create the new post. “The purpose of this role is to strengthen alignment across communications, external engagement and government relations so our colleges, divisions and administrative units are best positioned to advance their work and the university’s mission,” Hahn said in the email last week. Zak was most recently primary spokesman at the University of Arizona. Hahn had served as the U of A’s engineering college dean before he was hired as Boise State president on July 1. “Having worked with Mitch previously, I know firsthand his thoughtful, collaborative, servant leadership style, as well as his ability to build trusted relationships across complex organizations,” Hahn wrote. According to his biography on the U of A’s website, Zak has more than 30 years’ experience across the public and private sectors and nonprofits. “He has counseled two governors and numerous chief executives and shaped successful engagement programs for a wide range of organizations,” according to the website. Zak’s first day at Boise State will be Sept. 2. His salary will be $250,000 a year, Boise State spokeswoman Sherry Squires told Idaho Education News late Monday afternoon.

items.body: Tub of popcorn in hand and nestled into a recliner, Boise moviegoers may have seen the Boise School District’s new “Good Neighbor” commercial ahead of a summer blockbuster. The campaign is part of the district’s long-running investment in marketing, starting with $175,000 dedicated to the effort in 2018-19. The district is spending $150,000 this year on its marketing contract with Stoltz Marketing Group as it continues to try to retain and attract students — a challenge for Boise, which has seen the largest enrollment decline of any district in the state over the last five years, losing more than 1,600 students. The district has continued its partnership with Stoltz over the years, shifting campaigns to fit cultural moments. The “Good Neighbor” campaign was born out of the realization that 75% to 80% of Boise residents don’t have children in school, said Ryan Hill, district communications manager. The campaign’s goal is to show how Boise Schools impact the broader community. “We really wanted to specifically talk about not just our role as an educational institution and a great place for our kids to learn and grow,” Hill said. “(But) how the public schools are an integral part of our community.” Strong students grow up to have jobs the community needs, sports keep kids out of trouble, and connected school communities meet neighborhood needs, Hill said. Through the contract with Stoltz for various marketing campaigns, the ads will be featured in movie theaters and YouTube, Hulu, other streaming services and social media. Drivers may also see the ads on billboards. The campaign coincides with the Boise Schools Foundation’s recent push to do more marketing as it heads into its 40th anniversary year, said Jennifer Henderson, executive director. The foundation went through a strategic planning process last fall and decided to invest more in marketing and supporting the district’s efforts in that area. “‘Good Neighbor’ was really easy for us to attach ourselves to because that’s what we feel we are to the Boise Schools,” Henderson said. The foundation spent an additional $20,000 on its own set of videos, also produced by Stoltz, that coincide with the “Good Neighbor” campaign. The videos feature alumni who talk about the impact Boise Schools made on their lives. The district and foundation then share the footage for various projects. It can be hard for districts and foundations to set aside funds for marketing when the money could go toward directly serving students, Henderson said. But ultimately, she argued, it’s important — especially after the COVID-19 pandemic reshaped education for public schools to talk about their successes. “Unfortunately, negative stories get a lot more traction than the positive stories,” she said. “I think the deck is a little stacked toward private schools, or even when you hear charter schools that are putting money behind that.” While Boise Schools has a marketing and communications department of three people and a strong foundation to bolster its efforts, many school districts in the state don’t have a public information officer, adding communication duties to administrators’ plates. Communicating with the public often falls to administrators already juggling other responsibilities, making marketing a challenge for districts across the state. Still, more Idaho school districts are investing in communications. In 2020, 20 people in Idaho schools had “public information officer” in their job title. Now there are 38. Public schools are integral to creating good citizens, neighbors and communities, Henderson said. “Really what it’s about is telling our story,” Henderson said. “There is so much good going on in public schools.”

Opposition to the two ways that Green had her children, IVF and surrogacy, is rising. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Stateline) Brooke Green thought she needed a mammogram. Green, a Democratic state representative in Idaho, knew that breast cancer ran in her family and she “just had an inkling” that she should be tested. She was two weeks shy of the day her last remaining embryo would be implanted through in vitro fertilization. It was the one shot she had left to give her firstborn son a sibling, since it took several rounds of in vitro fertilization to get pregnant the first time. The mammogram confirmed her fears: There was in fact a lump in her breast, and a biopsy of the tumor confirmed it was cancer. Worse yet, it was a type of cancer fueled by estrogen and progesterone, two of the main hormones that skyrocket during pregnancy. She likely could not get pregnant and be treated for cancer at the same time. “The doctor’s file said if you had gotten pregnant, this could have been a disaster,” Green said. Several years earlier, Green had cosponsored bipartisan legislation , enacted in July 2023, codifying the best practices already in use by surrogacy agencies in Idaho, a state that has been called the unofficial capital of surrogacy in the United States. Last year, she found herself calling one of the agencies she’d worked with on the bill to ask for their help, this time as a client. She hired a surrogate to carry her second child, another boy, who was born in June. But opposition to the two ways that Green had her children, IVF and surrogacy, is rising. In the past two years, Republicans in Idaho and four other states have added specific anti-IVF language to their state party platforms, and some anti-abortion groups, including Students for Life of America and Live Action, have become increasingly outspoken in their opposition to both IVF and surrogacy. One reason is that many same-sex couples use both methods to have children, and many conservatives believe children should be raised by heterosexual married couples. Conservative critics also connect surrogacy to immigration, saying it facilitates “birth tourism” and birthright citizenship. And they note that IVF can involve the discarding of some embryos , which they say is akin to abortion. The latter is connected to the idea that a fetus or embryo is a person, with legal rights. As of June, lawmakers in at least 17 states had introduced 36 bills this year that would codify personhood rights for embryos or fetuses, according to the Guttmacher Institute, a reproductive rights advocacy group. Opponents were able to defeat them by arguing that they might limit IVF, which remains broadly popular. Idaho Democratic Rep. (Photo courtesy of Ashley Kirk-Robertson) Meanwhile in Washington, D.C., Republicans in Congress have blocked legislation that would directly protect IVF as a fertility treatment. (Getty Images) Editor’s note: This story was updated at 8:40 a.m. on Aug. 14 with a comment from the plaintiff in the legal challenge. It was updated again at 11: 10 a.m. with a comment fro
items.body: An Idaho federal judge blocked the Idaho attorney general and Ada County prosecutor from enforcing Idaho's abortion ban in cases where women face severe health risks or there's a high risk she may harm herself. (Getty Images) Editor’s note: This story was updated at 8:40 a.m. on Aug. 14 with a comment from the plaintiff in the legal challenge. It was updated again at 11: 10 a.m. with a comment from the Idaho attorney general. A pregnant woman may receive abortions in many cases if there are serious risks to her health or if there’s a high risk she will harm herself, an Idaho federal judge has ruled. The decision , released Thursday, marks a major change to the Idaho abortion ban’s exemptions. The judge determined U.S. constitutional protections under the Due Process and Equal Protection clauses of the 14th Amendment “establish a narrow but fundamental right to abortion when a pregnancy threatens the woman’s life or health.” U.S. District Court of Idaho Judge B. Lynn Winmill in his 81-page decision blocked the Idaho attorney general or Ada County prosecutor from enforcing Idaho’s criminal laws that prohibit providing abortions in narrow cases to protect the mother’s health. Initiative to end Idaho’s strict abortion ban qualifies for November’s general election ballot “By banning health-preserving abortion, Idaho attempts to deny this fundamental right on the basis that the threat of harm comes from a fetus, which depends on the woman for survival,” Winmill wrote. “But a pregnant woman’s health is not a state resource to be allocated at the legislature’s whim. The Fourteenth Amendment exists precisely to prevent subjugation like this.” His ruling largely favored the protections sought by Dr. Stacy Seyb, a Boise maternal-fetal medicine specialist, who challenged the state’s laws. He was represented by attorneys from the Lawyering Project and Legal Voice. “I have been caring for Idaho patients with high-risk pregnancies for nearly 30 years,” said Seyb said in a press release. “Today’s ruling allows me to once again offer patients with serious medical conditions the option of ending a pregnancy without leaving the state and to practice medicine without fear of criminal prosecution.” Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador, whose office defended Idaho’s abortion laws in court, said he plans to appeal the decision. “Judge Winmill did exactly what the Supreme Court rejected in Dobbs: he legislated from the bench and manufactured a new constitutional right to abortion,”Labrador said in an emailed statement. “The Supreme Court made clear that abortion policy belongs to the people and their elected representatives, not a single federal judge. Not only did he ignore Dobbs, he compounded that mistake by ignoring clear precedent stating that district judges lack authority to issue universal injunctions. We will appeal immediately, and we are confident this decision will be overturned.” The Idaho Family Policy Center, a Christian political advocacy group that opposes abortion, denounced the decision in a press release Thursday. The policy center helped author Idaho’s civil enforcement abortion law, which allows family members of an aborted fetus to sue the abortion provider for a minimum of $20,000. “It’s important to recognize that the civil cause of action in the Heartbeat law still remains in effect — meaning that any physician who performs an abortion that is prohibited by the Heartbeat law can still be liable for breaking the law,” policy center President Blaine Conzatti wrote in the press release. “And doctors should take note: The IFPC Legal Center stands ready to hold doctors accountable who illegally perform abortions.” Conzatti wrote that he expects the decision to be overturned, arguing that the U.S. Constitution does not protect abortions for mental health reasons. items.body: A cutthroat trout caught on a western Montana river. (Photo by Blair Miller, Daily Montanan) Yellowstone National Park on Wednesday lifted fishing restrictions on most of the park’s rivers and streams that have been in place since late July. On July 29, park officials implemented hoot-owl restrictions on all rivers and streams, prohibiting fishing from 2 p.m. to sunrise, due to high water temperatures and low stream flows. Now, officials say cooling weather and water conditions in the forecast are allowing for most of those restrictions to be suspended. The exception is along the Madison, Firehole and Gibbon (downstream of Norris Campground) rivers, where full fishing closures began on July 15 and will remain in effect until conditions improve further. These rivers run warmer due to the influence of nearby geothermal areas that increase water temperatures, a park press release stated. Staff will continue to monitor the water temperatures. The closures may be lifted, or additional restrictions and closures may be put in place, depending on condition assessments. For anglers, park officials recommend fishing during the coolest times of day and landing fish quickly. Do not play hooked trout to exhaustion, gently handle fish in water as much as possible, and let them recover before release. FWP eases hoot-owl restrictions across state Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks today also announced it will begin easing fishing restrictions on Aug. 13 for many waterways due to decreasing temperatures, but a section of the Big Hole River will see new restrictions due to low streamflows. items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Supreme Court building in Boise as seen on Jan. 14, 2026. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho Supreme Court Justice Robyn Brody will become chief justice of the Idaho Supreme Court effective Oct. 1, officials the Idaho Judicial Branch announced Thursday. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Brody, who was first elected to the Idaho Supreme Court in 2016, succeeds Chief Justice G. Richard Bevan, who is retiring Oct. 30. The Idaho Supreme Court is the highest court in the state, and Brody is set to become the second woman to serve as chief justice in Idaho, Idaho Judicial Branch officials said. Retired Justice Linda Copple Trout became the first woman to serve as chief justice of the Idaho Supreme Court in 1997. Brody currently serves as vice chief of the Idaho Supreme Court. Idaho Supreme Court Justice Robyn Brody will become chief justice on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Idaho Judicial Branch) “Idaho is a special place; the dedication and professionalism of our independent courts have helped make it so,” Brody said in a statement issued Thursday. “I am honored to serve our state in this way, and I am grateful for the trust of my fellow justices.” Brody has been a lawyer in Idaho for almost 30 years, and she started her own law firm in Rupert in 2010 prior to being elected to the Idaho Supreme Court. Brody has also been an adjunct law professor at the University of Idaho’s College of Law. Brody is chair of Idaho’s Pro Bono Commission and the Idaho Supreme Court’s Language Access Committee. She is also a board member of the Idaho Law Foundation, which oversees the Idaho Volunteer Lawyers Program and civic education programs, such as mock trials. Under the Idaho Constitution , the chief justice of the Idaho Supreme Court is selected via a majority vote of the Idaho Supreme Court. The chief justice is responsible for leading the court, judicial officials said. The Idaho Supreme Court’s chief justice is also the executive head of the state’s court system and works with other justices to manage that system. The chief justice also traditionally addresses the Idaho Legislature each year. Bevan has served as chief justice of the Idaho Supreme Court since 2021. On Thursday, he issued a statement expressing support for Brody. “Justice Brody has long worked to ensure that in a changing world, our courts remain accessible to all,” Bevan said. “Our Judicial Branch is in excellent hands.” YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. items.body: Even before the 2025 Legislature passed a sweeping anti-DEI law , the University of Idaho had eliminated five programs and cut 16 jobs. Boise State University, meanwhile, had shut down four programs and cut seven positions. Idaho’s diversity, equity and inclusion ban has had widely varying impacts across the state’s campuses — and in some cases, the changes began before the Legislature acted. Reports to the Legislature — required by the anti-DEI law — provide a school-by-school measuring stick. The Legislature required colleges and universities to review all offices and programs, staff positions and “trainings, activities, or courses of instruction,” dating back to 2023. The reports chronicle any staff jobs or campus activities that would have violated the DEI ban, had the law been on the books at the time. What about the impact on classes? The 2025 law generally forbids required “DEI-related” courses. There are exceptions, however — if a college or university has no suitable substitute in its syllabus, and the State Board of Education agrees to provide an exemption. The State Board granted 20 waivers for fall 2025; click here for in-depth coverage . Here are thumbnails from the campuses: U of I . In December 2024, before the Legislature’s DEI crackdown, the State Board of Education approved a policy restricting DEI-based programs. The U of I responded to the State Board within the month. The university closed its Office of Equity and Diversity, Office of Multicultural Affairs, Women’s Center, LGBTQA Office and Black/African American Cultural Center, and eliminated the 16 jobs that supported the programs. The U of I also eliminated an annual training requirement: a review of the university’s diversity statement. The statement no longer appears on the U of I website. Boise State . The four program shutdowns — affecting the Student Equity Center and the Gender Equity Center, among other programs — were done by November 2024 , even before the State Board passed its DEI policy. As a result, Boise State eliminated seven jobs. But the university later created three new positions, partly to staff its new Student Connections and Support Center , which was designed to replace the equity centers. Boise State also tweaked its new student orientation leader training program. One change eliminated a slide “referencing cultural differences of a wide breadth such as communication style, music choices, religion, race, gender, class, family background.” Idaho State University . Like Boise State, Idaho State made its changes before the State Board’s mandate. Idaho State closed its Diversity Resource Center and Janet C. Anderson Gender Resource Center in November 2024 — setting up a holistic center designed to support all students. The moves did not affect staffing; two employees were reassigned. Idaho State closed its Office of Equity and Inclusion. A new Office of Equal Opportunity and Title IX, reporting directly to the president, “continues important compliance responsibilities.” Lewis-Clark State College . No changes in programs, staffing or training. College of Western Idaho . Before the 2025 law went into effect, CWI closed two programs tailored to Hispanic students and a third program serving Hispanic employees. No changes in programs, staffing or training. NIC closed its diversity council in the spring of 2025. College of Eastern Idaho . The college said it “halted” all activities that could be defined as promoting DEI — such as its Unity Committee. (Photo by Valentin Termite/Idaho Capital Sun) On the morning of July 31, Idaho Organization of Resource Councils members Samantha Guerrero and Julia Santiago met at a Nampa Home Depot. Their cars, parked right next to each other, trunks open, were prepared for a distribution of aid to local farmworkers impacted by wildfire smoke and high summer temperatures. They carried crates of Gatorade, N95 masks, protective gloves, eyewear – basic supplies needed by farmworkers to carry out rough, often unforgiving agricultural work across the state. Soon, they would be driving 20 minutes away to a group of farmworkers combing through a corn cob field. Santiago and Guerrero said their mission, as well as that of the Idaho Organization of Resource Councils as an organization, is to provide rural immigrant workers with supplies needed for their day-to-day activities. To donate to the 2026 JJ Saldaña Heat and Smoke Relief Fund, go to https://givebutter.com/2026hsf . “Samantha and other members of Idaho Organization of Resource Councils noticed that there was a need for essential supplies, because there was essentially no organization that goes out to the fields and delivers gloves, masks, bandanas and water,” Santiago said in an interview with the Idaho Capital Sun. “One way they realized that they could help farmworkers was being able to purchase these items for them. That way, it is not coming from their paychecks.” The organization channels aid through the JJ Saldaña Heat and Smoke fund, a community-based program that collects donations, supplies and other items for distribution to farmworkers exposed to smoke and heat. The fund, which turned almost six years old, began during 2020 in an effort to help farmworkers with COVID-19 related expenses. During that time, undocumented workers could not receive stipends for medical or other necessities, so the fund stepped in to help, according to Guerrero. “It’s an injustice to have the people who help feed us not always be able to provide food for themselves, and that is definitely something we saw during the pandemic,” Guerrero said. “People who didn’t have access to food or couldn’t leave their house, or they lived in rural areas and couldn’t go out to get healthy food at the grocery store … It really made us aware of so many injustices that our farmworker community faces.” Since then, Santiago said they have “continued to do this fund to help farmworkers.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. items.body: Boise State University’s athletics department faces a budget deficit that could rise to $18 million this fiscal year, after the Broncos made a costly move to the Pac-12 and amid mounting demand to pay athletes. Boise State Athletic Director Jeramiah Dickey and other university officials told the State Board of Education about the projected deficit during the board’s meeting Thursday at Idaho State University. Board policy requires athletic departments to notify the State Board when they face a deficit. Boise State Athletics ended last fiscal year $2 million in the red, according to a written update shared with the State Board. The hole could have been deeper if not for an $11.5 million surplus from the prior year supported by revenue from the Broncos’ trip to the College Football Playoff and a lucrative Post Malone concert at Albertsons Stadium. Without similar backstops in the current fiscal year, the deficit could grow to between $14 million and $18 million, which could be covered by the university’s reserves, according to Thursday’s update. Boise State officials attributed the deficit to two factors: Revenue sharing. College athletes are now eligible for direct payments from universities — known as “revenue sharing” — in addition to sponsorship deals. And Boise State is facing pressure to hike payments as the Broncos aim to compete with higher-spending programs. Boise State, for the first time last fiscal year, paid athletes $10 million. University officials expect to increase payments this year, although they haven’t settled on a number. Dickey said Boise State could rank third or fourth in the Pac-12 when it comes to revenue sharing. Boise State Athletic Director Jeramiah Dickey “We are falling behind,” he said. Still, Boise State won’t reach the revenue-sharing cap established by House v. NCAA. The legal settlement that laid the ground rules for paying college players says universities can pay athletes up to $21.3 million this year. Boise State “will not approach that maximum,” according to the written statement shared with the State Board. “We don’t need what everyone else has,” Dickey said. “We just need more than we currently have.” Pac-12 move. The other budget pressure comes from Boise State’s move to the Pac-12 Conference, university officials told the State Board. In 2024, Boise State announced that it was joining the Pac-12 along with four other Mountain West Conference members — San Diego State, Fresno State, Utah State and Colorado State. The Mountain West sued the five schools, seeking $55 million in “exit fees.” It also sought $100 million from the Pac-12 for “poaching” its members. After a two-year legal battle, the parties settled this month for an undisclosed amount. The San Diego Union-Tribune reported that the total settlement was around $70 million, and the five universities are on the hook for just under $10 million each. According to a budget summary shared with the State Board this week, Boise State Athletics’ operating expenses went up about $7.6 million between FY 2025 and FY 2026, an increase attributed to the Mountain West Conference “exit.” University can cover athletics deficit with reserves. State Board Executive Director Jennifer White noted Thursday that the athletics department’s budget hole is not a “structural deficit” at the broader university. According to written comments from State Board staff, Boise State has “sufficient institutional reserves” to “absorb the projected deficit without adversely affecting the institution’s overall financial position.” It’s not uncommon for universities to subsidize sports; in fact, it’s the norm. A recent report from the Government Accountability Office found that 94% of Division I athletics programs lost money during the 2023-24 school year, and the median revenue gap was $20.6 million. items.body: Nine out of 10 McCall-Donnelly bus rides have been electric for the past two years — a point of pride for Superintendent Tim Thomas. The district was among the first in the country to pilot electric buses when it received them a couple years ago, Thomas told EdNews. Electric school buses are popping up in more Idaho districts, thanks largely to federal grants that have helped them overcome upfront costs. McCall-Donnelly and the Genesee district were early Idaho recipients, and their experiences offer a glimpse of what other districts can expect as they make the switch. On Aug. 26, the Boise School District will unveil eight new electric buses for its own fleet, purchased with funds from a $2.76 million U.S. Environmental Protection Agency grant in 2024. The Horseshoe Bend district received a $400,000 grant the same year. ‘We’re 90% electric, and it works’ In 2022, McCall-Donnelly and Genesee received funds from the $1.2 trillion Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. McCall-Donnelly received $3.95 million for 10 buses and Genesee got $1.185 million for three buses. Both purchased electric models from IC Bus, a manufacturer that makes both electric and conventional buses. When the often-snowy McCall-Donnelly district received the grant money from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, it gave the money to then-contractor Harlow’s Bus Service in McCall to purchase and operate the buses. But McCall-Donnelly’s harsh winter weather presented a challenge: Harlow’s had to mount heaters and automatic tire chains, or drop-down chains, on the buses. “Harlow’s didn’t really want to do the work to figure out how to make them work up here,” Thomas said, “so we did.” In June 2025, McCall-Donnelly and Harlow’s negotiated a separation agreement. The district took direct ownership of the buses and created a transportation department. items.title: Idaho schools are losing thousands of students even as the state grows
items.summary: Idaho school enrollment has fallen by more than 5,000 students since reaching a peak in 2022-23, despite continued population growth across the state. items.body: Idaho school enrollment has fallen by more than 5,000 students since reaching a peak in 2022-23, despite continued population growth across the state. The decline is concentrated among elementary students, while enrollment continues to grow in middle and high schools. The shifting demographics impact K-12 funding and have contributed to school staffing adjustments, budget tightening and long-term plan changes. But Idaho’s enrollment story looks different depending on where families live and the choices available to them. Declines are more pronounced in some communities, while Idaho’s charter schools continue to grow and some traditional districts are buoying enrollment through online offerings. Here’s a closer look at the numbers and trends driving the changes. The big picture: Idaho is growing but enrollment is not Over the last five years, the state’s population increased from around 1.9 million residents to just over 2 million, according to U.S. Census Bureau data . Yet K-12 enrollment has fallen by 5,104 students since reaching a peak of 315,254 in fall 2022. Enrollment stood at 310,150 this fall. The decline has been concentrated in the lower grades, with K-3 enrollment falling by 5,151 students since 2021-22, according to Idaho Department of Education data. Here’s a closer look at the numbers by grade: The decrease is due in part to declining birth rates, which fell from over 16 per 1,000 residents in 2007 to under 12 per 1,000 residents in 2024, according to U.S. census data. Most of Idaho’s growth has come from people without school-aged children moving to the state, said Idaho Department of Labor Economist Lisa Grigg. According to Grigg, just 8% of Idaho’s population growth from 2020 to 2025 is attributed to school-aged children. Enrollment changes accompany budget challenges State funding for schools is calculated largely using average daily attendance. Declining enrollment does not always mean a funding loss, but fewer students attending school can reduce the attendance counts that drive state funding. Overall, average daily attendance and statewide K-12 funding disbursements have increased in recent years. And lawmakers kept state K-12 funding for this school year largely flat. But when attendance does decline at a district or charter, it can lose funding while many fixed costs remain. Many school leaders say that’s the challenge with the state’s enrollment-based model. Attendance-based funding reduces state revenue when more students are absent amid declining enrollment, but costs for things like busing and food services remain — and increase with inflation. Many school leaders say switching to an enrollment-based model would help schools stabilize funding. About 291,494 students attended school per day last school year, compared to the 309,254 students enrolled in public schools. That’s a gap of 17,760 students — or roughly $172.2 million if the state funded each of those students at about the same per-student rate. Idaho’s attendance-based funding formula is both complex and outdated, Idaho officials say . An effort to rewrite the more than 30-year-old formula is again in the works by state officials. The state offers some protection under the attendance-based model. Thirty-eight districts ended fiscal year 2026 in “protected” mode, meaning they can’t lose more than 3% from the prior year’s funding as attendance fluctuates from year to year. Districts adjust as enrollment falls The Boise School District has seen the largest enrollment decline in the state over the last five years, with a drop of more than 1,600 students. To adjust, Boise is cutting 17 staffing positions ahead of the 2026-27 school year. District spokesperson Dan Hollar said the reductions align staff levels with student needs: “The district’s approach is to align staffing with enrollment while preserving classroom instruction and essential student services whenever possible.” The decline is partly demographic. items.body: As campaigns for and against a proposed voter initiative that would repeal Idaho's abortion ban ramp up, an anti-abortion advocacy group has begun to question whether Idaho OB-GYNs have left the state since it went into effect. The state says it's hard to track, and doctors say the effect has been real. (Thanasis Zovoilis/Getty Images) Editor’s note: This story was updated at 2:24 p.m. Aug. 12 with comments from the Idaho Family Policy Center. Dr. Kylie Cooper, a maternal-fetal medicine physician, practices in Minnesota after she left Idaho in the spring of 2023, shortly after Idaho’s criminal abortion ban went into effect. Dr. Kylie Cooper, a maternal fetal medicine specialist .(Photo courtesy of Kylie Cooper) Although it has been nearly three years since she left, Cooper retained her Idaho medical license, she said. “I have a sliver of hope that maybe things will get better in the future,” Cooper said. Cooper’s license, as well as every other active medical OB-GYN license in the state, would have shown up in data recently shared by the Idaho Family Policy Center — a Christian advocacy group that lobbied for Idaho’s criminal abortion ban and helped author a 2022 law allowing family members of a fetus aborted after six weeks to the sue the abortion provider for a minimum of $20,000. As campaigns for and against Proposition 1 — a citizen-led ballot initiative that would repeal the state’s strict abortion ban and provide protections for contraception and in vitro fertilization, ramp up for the Nov. 3 general election — the abortion law’s effect on the number of practicing OB-GYNs in Idaho has become a talking point. But determining the true number of doctors providing obstetrician-gynecologist care in the state isn’t easy. The state has said the number of active licenses do not reliably reflect how many OB-GYNs are currently practicing in Idaho. The Idaho Family Policy Center has underscored the licensing data to question, and file a lawsuit over, a 2025 Boise State University study that found Idaho had lost 35% of its OB-GYNs since 2022, when the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade and Idaho’s criminal abortion law went into effect. The Idaho Family Policy Center posted this graph on Facebook Aug. 3. (Screenshot) The policy center on Aug. 3 posted a graph on Facebook showing the number of active licenses increasing from 2022 to 2025, writing “Pro-abortion advocates are lying to you.” “The number of actively licensed OB/GYNs in Idaho has actually increased since our pro-life laws went into effect, according to data from the Idaho Board of Medicine,” the post said. The center’s posts about the licensure numbers have been shared by Idaho state legislators, such as Twin Falls Republican Rep. Clint Hostetler and Middleton Republican Rep. Tammy Nichols. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Idaho medical board says it has no ‘reliable way’ to count active physicians The Idaho Board of Medicine, which is under the state Division of Occupational and Professional Licenses, shows the number of active OB-GYN licenses in Idaho going from around 280 in 2022 to just under 340 in 2024, according to the policy center’s graph . Bob McLaughlin, spokesperson at the Division of Occupational and Professional Licenses, known as DOPL, told the Idaho Capital Sun that there are limitations to the state’s data to try and determine how many doctors are practicing in the state. “1. It’s a two year license,” McLaughlin said in an email. “The number of licenses could fluctuate since the licensee is required to renew on their birthdate every two years and not annually. 2. Physician specialty information is self-reported and is not required as part of licensure. DOPL does not have a reliable way to determine how many licensed physicians are actively practicing in Idaho. 3. Our records reflect licensure status, and an active license does not necessarily mean an individual is currently practicing.” Home Family policy center President Blaine Conzatti wrote

items.body: Boise trustee Nancy Gregory is leaving the school board after nearly two-and-a-half decades of service. Gregory received a distinguished service award and congratulations from her colleagues during her final night on the district dais Monday. “I’ve always had a passion for education, I was that PTO (parent-teacher organization) volunteer mom for years and years … The big picture, the strategic planning work has always been very interesting to me,” Gregory told EdNews after the meeting. She ran for the school board in 2002, when her first child went into junior high school. Gregory’s service on the board is ending, but her political career is not over: She’ll focus on her Senate campaign in District 15, a stretch of largely suburban areas between Boise and Meridian, currently represented by Republican Codi Galloway. Gregory, a Democrat, has received more than $55,000 in campaign contributions ahead of the Nov. 3 election, according to Idaho Sunshine. She feels uniquely prepared to take her experience to the Statehouse, having worked closely with legislators for decades on committees or with the Idaho School Boards Association, “fighting for causes that are important to education,” she said. “I look into the future, and I see, as in the past, the target has been on our backs in some regards,” Gregory said, referring to public education, after receiving her award. “I think we have champions who will stand up for us in this community.” The board also discussed refinancing a bond during Monday’s meeting and heard details about the district’s new website. items.body: CORRECTION: A previous version of this article said Senate Bill 1366 created the new civics test requirement. That was false. The correct legislation is Senate Bill 1336. A new Idaho high school civics test, taking effect in 2027-28, will test students’ knowledge of American government, history and the Constitution — but the 50-question exam is more than a stroll through the basics. It begins with 12 short-answer, written-response questions, followed by 38 multiple-choice questions. Students must score at least 60% to pass but can retake the test as many times as needed. How well do you know your civics? Take our quiz with questions from the new test. Idaho already requires students to pass a civics test for graduation, but the new exam will replace the previous 100-question citizenship test. The new test was introduced after some lawmakers raised concerns about civics instruction in Idaho schools. It will assess students’ knowledge of American government, the nation’s founding principles and constitutional amendments. The Idaho Department of Education says the new test is “more rigorous than the previous version” and that educators “may need to adjust instruction and assessment in high school U.S. History and U.S. Government courses” to ensure students are prepared. Here are some of the questions: Define the concept of democracy. Define the concept of liberty. Explain the benefits of a bicameral legislature. Despite having half as many questions as the prior exam the new test is meant to be tougher. The previous test was “trivial,” said Rep. Tony Wisniewski, who proposed a new civics test in 2025. Discussion shifted during last legislative session from frustration with the status quo to concerns about anti-American views in schools. “We need to do something to help get our young people back (to) loving our country,” said sponsoring Rep. Barbara Ehardt, R-Idaho Falls. “It is impossible to teach somebody to love our country by teaching them propaganda that is antithetical to how this country came about.” Parade watchers and participants before the Idaho State Capitol building during Boise’s America 250 parade on July 4, 2026. (Kaeden Lincoln/EdNews) " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/independenceday1-1180x885.jpg" class="size-full wp-image-122573" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/independenceday1.jpg" alt="" width="1920" height="1440" srcset="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/independenceday1.jpg 1920w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/independenceday1-620x465.jpg 620w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/independenceday1-1180x885.jpg 1180w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/independenceday1-200x150.jpg 200w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/independenceday1-1536x1152.jpg 1536w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1920px) 100vw, 1920px" /> Parade watchers and participants before the Idaho State Capitol building during Boise’s America 250 parade on July 4, 2026. (Kaeden Lincoln/EdNews) The test requires students to articulate the United States’ multiparty lawmaking process. The legislation creating the new test requirement, Senate Bill 1336 in 2026, passed with only Republican support. Critics have complained the legislation bypassed the usual method of changing academic content standards: a multiple-year endeavor starting with a standards writing committee and followed by public, State Board and legislative review. “By putting standards into code, we essentially make them political artifacts and not educational ones,” said Sen.
